extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalists, policymakers and students interested in Brazil's media/technology/political landscape
extracted.subtask_description: A country-level analytical report describing Brazil's news ecosystem, including audience metrics, trust measures, platform use, regulatory developments, industry economics, journalist safety, and AI-related policies. Useful for understanding how political polarisation and technology shape news consumption and industry health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political polarisation as a media-environment factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Brazil’s politics remains deeply polarised following close-run elections in 2022 and subsequent attempts to overturn the result, which included riots and the storming of the National Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polarisation is presented as a contextual criterion that affects news agendas, public trust, and audience behaviour; supported by survey data (Quaest) showing 83% of Brazilians believed the country was more divided than united in Feb 2024 (up from 64% six months earlier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media ownership concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Media ownership remains concentrated, with a number of large, privately owned conglomerates running outlets across broadcast, print, and online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration is a structural evaluative dimension: these conglomerates are under pressure as audience habits change, implying implications for plurality, diversity, and resilience of news provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: News avoidance (audience disengagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of respondents who avoid news often or sometimes reached 47%, up from 41% last year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News avoidance is treated as a key audience metric potentially driven by a 'heavyweight news agenda' (political conflict plus international crises). High avoidance rates indicate challenges for reach and civic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform weekly reach and changing audience habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly reach of all the main news sources has declined in the past few years, including social media, where all the main networks have been on a downward path, except for TikTok.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use weekly reach trends to evaluate platform importance; note exceptions (TikTok growth) and consider celebrity/influencer follower counts (e.g., TV Globo ~6 million vs comedian Whindersson Nunes 22.4 million) when assessing competitive dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in social platforms for news
rubrics_metrics.description: In our survey, TikTok and X are considered the least trustworthy of the top networks for news – 24% of users of both platforms say it’s difficult to tell trustworthy and untrustworthy news content apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-level trust perceptions are an explicit evaluative metric; low trustability scores signal platform-specific credibility issues that affect news consumption and may influence newsroom strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory attempts regarding digital platforms and misinformation (fake news bill)
rubrics_metrics.description: There was an unsuccessful attempt to pass a bill regulating digital platforms and misinformation last year. The tech firms fiercely opposed the ‘fake news bill’, which would make digital platforms responsible for preventing the spread of falsehoods and hate speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory proposals and political responses are evaluative factors when assessing the national media governance environment; note that strong industry opposition (e.g., Google placing a homepage link opposing the law) can shape outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral regulation on synthetic media (deepfake ban and AI labelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Electoral Court issued a ruling banning deepfakes from official election campaign material and ruled that any synthetic multimedia content should have a label stating it was created using AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal requirements on campaign content and mandatory AI labelling are concrete regulatory standards affecting content producers and platforms; they serve as compliance criteria for political advertising and synthetic media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher policies on AI use and data access
rubrics_metrics.description: Editora Globo barred AI companies from crawling its content to train their generative models; conversely, some outlets are experimenting with AI products (e.g., O Estado de S. Paolo launched a chatbot using its previously published content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher-level policies (blocking data scraping, experimentation with chatbots) are criteria for evaluating industry responses to generative AI—ranging from protective measures to product innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper circulation metrics and methodology sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The downward trend in circulation for the newspaper industry was reversed last year, but mainly as a result of a change in the criteria used to calculate the number of online subscribers; even readers who paid extremely low promotional prices were now considered subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation/subscriber figures must be interpreted in light of methodological changes; evaluators should check definitions and counting rules to avoid misleading conclusions about industry health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism labour market (hires vs. job losses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A study showed that while 9,500 professionals were hired last year, 10,400 jobs were lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Net employment change is an economic health indicator for the news industry; consider both hires and redundancies to assess stability and workforce trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety of journalists (attacks and violence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The federation found that the number of attacks against journalists fell by 52% to 181. The figures include physical aggression, threats, legal decisions restricting the freedom of press, and journalist arrests, among other types of violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalist safety is a multi-dimensional criterion including physical, legal, and digital threats; declines/increases in attacks are important markers of press freedom and working conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall trust in news (national metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust in news overall: 43% (unchanged from last year), and Brazil ranks first among the six Latin American countries surveyed in this dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overall trust percentage and cross-country rank to assess public confidence in news institutions; track year-on-year changes for trend analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to pay for online news
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportion paying for online news is an economic/engagement metric for evaluating business model viability and audience monetisation potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom index position and score (RSF)
rubrics_metrics.description: RSF World Press Freedom Index: 82/180, Score 58.59 (measure of press freedom from Reporters Without Borders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International index scores provide comparative benchmarks for press freedom and are useful alongside domestic indicators (safety, legal constraints, ownership concentration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of high-profile personalities on news reach
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile personalities (e.g., Lula and Bolsonaro) and influencers have large followings on platforms like TikTok, outpacing traditional news brands in follower counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the role of influencers/political actors in the information ecosystem—count follower reach and platform influence as part of audience and competition analysis.
